pages.text: On a school trip to a museum, Delasi put on white gloves. Mr Gyamfi, the guide, placed a tiny object in her palm. It was a clay animal no longer than her thumb. “A dog,” said Nyamekye. “Maybe,” said Mr Gyamfi. “It was made by people who lived near Kintampo more than three thousand years ago.”

Mr Gyamfi, the guide, placed a tiny object in her palm.
It was a clay animal no longer than her thumb.
“A dog,” said Nyamekye.
“Maybe,” said Mr Gyamfi.
“It was made by people who lived near Kintampo more than three thousand years ago.”
pages.alt: A girl in gloves holds a tiny clay animal while a guide watches.

pages.text: “We call them the Kintampo people, or the Kintampo complex,” said Mr Gyamfi. “Their sites are mostly in the Bono East region of Ghana, around towns like Nkoranza and Techiman, and some are found in nearby countries.” “How old are they?” asked Nyamekye. “Ah,” said Mr Gyamfi, with a twinkle. “That is a puzzle of its own. Wait for page four.”

pages.text: “How do we know what they ate?” asked Delasi. “From burnt seeds and bones,” said Mr Gyamfi. “Archaeologists found charred pearl millet, and signs of oil palm, yams and cowpea. They found bones of goats, sheep, cattle and dogs, and also wild animals such as antelope and guineafowl. Traces show rectangular houses made of wattle and daub.” Delasi wrote: farmers, herders and hunters.

pages.text: “Now the date puzzle,” said Mr Gyamfi. “One source says the Kintampo complex lasted from about 2500 to 1400 BCE. A review by an archaeologist named D. J. Watson says the tradition appeared about 3,600 to 3,200 years ago. Those are not the same.” Nyamekye did the sum: 3,600 years ago is about 1600 BCE. “So they overlap, but they do not match,” he said.

pages.text: Mr Gyamfi turned back to the clay dog. “Clay animals like this one have been found at places such as Boyase Hill and Ntereso, shaped like dogs, lizards and cows. And here is the mystery: nobody knows exactly why they were made.” “A toy?” guessed Nyamekye. “A gift? A story?” said Delasi. “All possible,” said Mr Gyamfi, “but we cannot prove any of them.”

pages.text: “And where did the people come from?” asked Delasi. “That is another question,” said Mr Gyamfi. “Some archaeologists think the Kintampo people came from further north, from the Sahel or Sahara, and brought new ways of living. Others think local people changed their lifestyle. Both ideas are still debated. And remember the dates: nobody agrees yet, so scientists keep asking. Maybe different sites give different ages. Maybe scientists count the start and the end in different ways. Maybe the dating methods are corrected in different ways. Those are guesses, not answers.”

pages.text: “So what do we really know?” asked Nyamekye. Delasi made a list. Known: pottery, tools, seeds and bones show people farmed, herded and hunted here. Debated: where they came from. Unknown: the meaning of the clay animals. “Clues,” she said, “and then honest guesses.”

pages.text: Before leaving, Delasi held the clay dog one more time. “Someone shaped this with their fingers,” she said. “They did not know us, but they left a message.” Mr Gyamfi smiled. “That is why we protect these places,” he said, “and why we ask people never to take objects from ancient sites.” The end.
